title: Design typeahead / autocomplete
scopeHtml: Scope: trie vs prefix index, top-k, offline aggregation, caching, update pipeline, sharding.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Typeahead (autocomplete) suggests completions as the user types: typing "iph" shows "iphone 15", "iphone case"... Google Search, Amazon, Swiggy's dish search and the Android address bar all do it. It must feel instant: suggestions arrive before the next keystroke.

Functional

  • Given a prefix, return the top K (for example 5 to 10) suggestions ranked by popularity.
  • Update suggestions as search trends change (hourly or daily, plus breaking trends faster).
  • Optional: personalisation, typo tolerance, language support, filtering offensive terms.

Non-functional

  • Very low latency: p99 under 100 ms end to end (aim for under 50 ms server side).
  • Highly available; stale suggestions are acceptable (eventual consistency).
  • Handles huge read traffic; writes (new data) are offline batch.

Decision gravity. Treat it as a read-heavy system with an offline-built index. This frees you from real-time writes and is reversible. A fully real-time system (update on every query) is a much costlier path.

Everyday analogy. A phone's contact search: the moment you type "Ra" it narrows down to Rahul, Raj, Ravi, best matches first.

Common interview traps.

  • Querying the main search database with LIKE 'iph%' on each keystroke.
  • Not defining "top K by what" (popularity, recency, personal).
  • Ignoring that most requests are for a few very common prefixes.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
GET /v1/suggest?q=iph&limit=5&lang=en&userId=42
200 OK
{ "prefix": "iph",
  "suggestions": [
    { "text": "iphone 15",      "score": 98211 },
    { "text": "iphone 15 case", "score": 51230 },
    { "text": "iphone charger", "score": 30112 },
    { "text": "iphone 14",      "score": 29001 },
    { "text": "iphone price",   "score": 18877 } ] }
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300
POST /internal/events/search    (async, batched from client or backend)
{ "query": "iphone 15", "ts": 1731150000, "userId": 42, "selectedSuggestion": true }
202 Accepted

Client-side behaviour matters as much as the API:

  • Debounce 100 to 150 ms so fast typing does not send a request per key.
  • Cancel in-flight requests when a new key is typed.
  • Cache results per prefix in the client (and a short browser cache via headers).
  • Trigger only after the first 1 to 2 characters.

Industry example. Google returns suggestions within roughly tens of ms using prefix caches at the edge; Amazon blends popularity with personalisation.

Everyday analogy. A helpful shop assistant who starts guessing your order after the first syllable.

Common interview traps.

  • No debounce, so 5x the necessary QPS.
  • Returning huge payloads rather than K short strings.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 500M searches/day, average query 20 characters, 100M daily active users.

Quantity Calculation Result
Searches/s 500M / 86,400 about 5,800/s
Typeahead requests/s each search triggers ~5 requests after debounce ~29k/s, peak ~90k/s
Distinct queries kept top 100M distinct queries (long tail pruned) 100M
Avg query size 25 bytes 2.5 GB raw strings
Trie / index memory with structure overhead ~5x 10 to 15 GB
Response size 5 x ~30 B + JSON ~300 B
Egress 90k/s x 300 B ~27 MB/s (tiny)

The data fits in the RAM of one machine, so the real concern is read QPS and availability, solved by replication and caching, not sharding by size. Shard only for geographic or language reasons, or to cut per-node QPS.

Everyday analogy. The whole phone book fits on one desk; the issue is how many people ask it questions at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Estimating all queries ever typed instead of pruning the long tail (queries seen fewer than N times).
  • Forgetting the 5x multiplier from keystrokes.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Two paths

  1. Read path (hot): request to edge cache, then suggestion servers that hold the whole index in memory. Latency is a hash lookup.
  2. Build path (offline): search events go through Kafka into a batch/stream aggregator (Spark/Flink) that counts queries per window, applies filters, builds the index (trie or precomputed prefix map) and publishes a snapshot (for example to S3). Servers load the new snapshot and swap atomically.

Decision gravity. Offline-built immutable snapshots make the serving layer simple and fast, and a bad index can be rolled back by loading the previous snapshot (two-way door). The cost is freshness: trends appear after the next build (hourly). Mitigate with a small real-time overlay.

Industry examples. Google blends precomputed popular completions with real-time trending queries; Twitter's search needed real-time trending, so it added a fast overlay for hot topics.

Everyday analogy. A printed menu reprinted every morning, plus a whiteboard for today's specials.

Common interview traps.

  • Updating the serving index in place on every event (locks, contention).
  • No rollback story for a bad data build.

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Data structure: trie vs precomputed map

A trie stores characters as a tree; every path from the root spells a prefix. To return the top K for prefix "iph", walk 3 nodes, then find the best K under that node.

Naive: DFS the whole subtree and sort: far too slow for prefixes like "a". Fix: store the top K at every node (precomputed), making a query O(length of prefix).

root
 └ i
    └ ip
       └ iph  top5: [iphone 15 (98k), iphone 15 case (51k), iphone charger (30k), ...]

Memory cost: K strings (or IDs) per node. Save memory by storing query IDs (4 bytes) instead of strings and compress single-child chains (a radix / compressed trie).

Alternative: flat hash map prefix -> [top K list] for all prefixes up to length ~10-15. Simpler and works well in a cache like Redis (GET sug:iph). More memory (every prefix stored), fewer pointers, trivially shardable. This is the pragmatic choice at this scale.

Trie with top K Prefix to list map
Lookup O(prefix length) O(1) hash
Memory Lower (shared prefixes) Higher
Sharding Harder Trivial by prefix hash
Typo support Possible via edit-distance traversal Needs separate index

Ranking: what is the score?

Start with query frequency in a trailing window (for example 7 days), with time decay so old popularity fades: score = sum(count_d x 0.9^(age_days)). Blend:

  • global popularity (main signal),
  • recency/trending boost (spike ratio against baseline),
  • personalisation (user's history, location, language) applied by re-ranking the top 20 from the shared index down to 5,
  • safety filters (blocklist of offensive queries, legal removals).

Building and updating the index

  1. Clients and the search service log queries (and whether a suggestion was clicked) to Kafka.
  2. A job (Spark hourly, or Flink with 5-minute windows) counts queries; drops those seen fewer than, say, 5 times (spam and typos).
  3. Builds prefix to top-K and writes a versioned snapshot index-2026-11-09-14.bin.
  4. Servers download the new file, build in memory beside the old, and swap a pointer atomically (no downtime, no locks on the read path).
  5. Keep the last 3 snapshots for instant rollback.

Trending overlay: a small in-memory structure (Count-Min sketch + heap) fed by a stream tracks queries spiking right now; the server merges those into the top K at request time.

Caching layers

  • Browser/client cache: Cache-Control: max-age=300 plus local prefix cache.
  • CDN/edge cache keyed by prefix: for short prefixes (1 to 3 chars) a few thousand keys serve most traffic, so hit rate is very high (90%+).
  • Server in-memory index answers the rest in microseconds.

Sharding and replication

The index fits on one node (~10 to 15 GB), so replicate rather than shard: 10 identical servers behind a load balancer each handle ~9k/s at peak. Shard only if the data grows (multilingual: shard by language/region) using prefix-range partitioning; avoid sharding by first letter since "s" and "a" are far busier than "x" (hot shard). Geo-replicate so users hit a nearby region.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: users see offensive or stale suggestions. Metric: blocklist hit counts, index version age. Fix: a separate fast "denylist" applied at serve time that does not wait for a rebuild.

Typo tolerance and extras

Add a fuzzy layer (edit distance 1 to 2 via a BK-tree, or n-gram index in Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) only if required; mention that it costs latency and memory. For multi-language, normalise Unicode and tokenise per language.

Everyday analogy. The trie with top K at each node is a library where every shelf label already lists the five most borrowed books beyond that shelf.

Common interview traps.

  • Computing top K on the fly by traversing the subtree.
  • Sharding by first letter and creating hot shards.
  • Rebuilding the trie in place under live traffic.
  • Skipping the safety/blocklist step.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Clear separation of the read path (fast, in-memory, cached) and the offline update path.
  • The trie with top-K per node idea, and when a plain prefix map is preferable.
  • Concrete numbers: QPS with debounce, index size, why one machine's RAM is enough.
  • Caching at several layers; client-side debouncing.
  • Ranking beyond raw counts: decay, trending, personalisation, filtering.
  • Atomic snapshot swap and rollback.
  • Seniors discuss freshness vs cost, hot shards, multi-language, privacy (do not suggest one user's private queries to others; minimum count thresholds) and A/B testing of ranking with click-through metrics.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating it as a pure database problem rather than a latency and caching problem.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Typeahead is read-heavy with an offline-built index: prefix to top K suggestions.
  • Estimate with debounce: ~29k/s average, ~90k/s peak; index around 10 to 15 GB, so replicate rather than shard.
  • Store top K at every trie node (or a prefix-to-list map) so a query is O(prefix length) or O(1).
  • Build via Kafka, aggregation, snapshot, atomic swap; keep old snapshots for rollback; add a trending overlay and a live denylist.
  • Cache at client, CDN and server; debounce and cancel requests on the client.
  • Offline snapshots are a reversible choice; freshness is the price.

questions.promptHtml: How do you return the top 5 suggestions for a prefix quickly? Why not just traverse the trie subtree?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The core trick of the problem; separates memorised from understood.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Store the precomputed top K at every trie node. A query then walks as many nodes as the prefix is long and returns the stored list: O(prefix length). Traversing the subtree and sorting is far too slow for a short prefix like "a", which sits above millions of queries.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
root
 └ i
    └ ip
       └ iph  top5: [iphone 15 (98k), iphone 15 case (51k), iphone charger (30k), ...]
  • Memory: K entries per node. Reduce by storing 4-byte query ids instead of strings and compressing single-child chains (radix trie).
  • Alternative: flat map prefix -> top-K list for prefixes up to length 10-15: O(1) lookup, easy to shard and put in Redis (GET sug:iph) but uses more memory.
Trie with top K Prefix map
Lookup O(prefix length) O(1)
Memory Lower Higher
Sharding Harder Trivial by prefix hash

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Computing top K on the fly from the subtree.
  • Storing full strings in every node.
  • Rebuilding the trie in place under live traffic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which would you choose at 100M queries? -> The prefix map or trie, both fit in 10 to 15 GB; I pick the map for simplicity unless memory is tight.
  2. How do you update counts? -> Offline rebuild into a new snapshot, not in-place.
  3. Typos? -> Separate fuzzy index (edit distance, n-gram) costing latency and memory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use a trie". Senior: top-K per node, memory tricks and when a flat map is better.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team computed top-K with DFS per request and timed out on one-letter prefixes.

questions.subtopic: Offline index build and atomic swap
questions.promptHtml: Why build the suggestion index offline in snapshots, and how do you publish a new one without downtime or a bad release?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests separation of read and build paths and rollback thinking.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Reads are the hot path and need a simple, immutable, in-memory index. So search events flow through Kafka to an aggregation job that counts queries, filters them and builds a versioned snapshot in S3. Servers load it beside the old one and swap a pointer atomically, and I keep the last few snapshots for instant rollback. The price is freshness, which I cover with a small real-time trending overlay.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Search events -> Kafka -> Aggregate counts -> Build trie -> Snapshot -> Servers swap
  • Aggregator (Spark hourly or Flink 5-minute windows) drops queries seen fewer than about 5 times (spam, typos).
  • Snapshot name like index-2026-11-09-14.bin; servers build in memory next to the live index, then swap.
  • Rollback: load the previous snapshot; it is a two-way door.
  • Overlay: Count-Min sketch plus heap for queries spiking right now, merged at request time.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Updating the live index per event (locks, contention).
  • No rollback story.
  • Skipping the safety filters in the build.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Memory during swap? -> Two copies briefly; 10-15 GB each, plan for it.
  2. How do you validate a snapshot? -> Size sanity checks, sample queries, canary on one server.
  3. How fresh is fresh enough? -> Business decision; hourly plus overlay is typical.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: describes the batch job. Senior: atomic swap, rollback, overlay, validation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bad build removed half the suggestions; rollback to the previous snapshot restored service in minutes.

questions.contextHtml: 100M DAU, 500M searches/day, average query 20 characters, users get suggestions after the first character with client debounce of about 150 ms. Interviewer: "does this need sharding?"
questions.promptHtml: Estimate QPS, index size and answer the sharding question.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Says "billions of queries, shard by first letter".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Languages? Personalisation? Do we keep the long tail?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The data fits in RAM; the concern is read QPS and availability.
  4. How I'd verify each: 500M / 86,400 = about 5,800 searches/s; each triggers about 5 requests after debounce: about 29k/s, peak about 90k/s. Keep the top 100M distinct queries (prune the tail): 100M x 25 B = 2.5 GB, with trie overhead about 5x = 10 to 15 GB. Response about 300 B, egress about 27 MB/s.
  5. Root cause: N/A.
  6. Fix: Replicate rather than shard: 10 identical servers behind an LB, each about 9k/s at peak; CDN and client caches cut a large share before that. Shard only for language or region, or per-node QPS.
  7. Prevention: Load tests at 2x peak; memory alert on index size.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not shard by first letter; "s" and "a" are far busier than "x" (hot shard).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Index grows to 500 GB (many languages)? -> Shard by language or region, prefix-range partitioning inside.
  • No debounce? -> About 5x QPS.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team sharded a 12 GB index across 20 nodes and spent months on cross-shard top-K merging for no gain.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no numbers.
  • Hire: QPS with debounce, index fits in RAM, replicate.
  • Strong hire: hot-shard reasoning and when sharding is justified.

questions.contextHtml:
A news event makes an offensive, defamatory query trend; it appears as suggestion #2 for a person's name. Hourly index build is 40 minutes from finishing and then publishes. Legal wants it gone in minutes. Index version age is 14 hours (a build failed overnight and nobody noticed).

index_version_age: 14h   last_good_build: 2026-11-08T22:00
blocklist file updated: 2026-11-09T11:58 (not applied; applied at build time only)
questions.promptHtml: What do you do now, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rebuild the index" or "wait for the next build".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the term in cache layers too (CDN, client)? How many queries match? Any legal timelines?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Push the term to a live denylist applied at serve time; purge CDN keys for affected prefixes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Blocklist only applied in build; build failure undetected; edge cache holds stale results (max-age 300).
  4. How I'd verify each: Query the API for those prefixes at origin and via the CDN; job logs for the failed build.
  5. Root cause: Safety filtering coupled to a slow batch path, no freshness alert.
  6. Fix: Serve-time denylist (small, hot-reloaded), applied after retrieving top-K; CDN invalidation for affected prefixes; fix the build and alert on index version age over threshold.
  7. Prevention: Alert at 2x the build interval; test blocklist with a canary query; an on-call runbook.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not over-block by dropping entire prefixes; I would not rely on the build alone for safety. Denylist matching adds microseconds.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Names of real people (privacy)? -> Minimum count thresholds, removal on request.
  • False positives in the denylist? -> Review process and audit log.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A failed overnight build served 14-hour-old suggestions during breaking news; the freshness alert did not exist.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: waits for the build.
  • Hire: serve-time denylist and cache purge.
  • Strong hire: alerting on index age, runbook, privacy considerations.

questions.contextHtml:
The suggestion fleet has 40 servers and costs a lot; peak is 90k req/s. CDN hit rate is only 22%, and p99 at origin is 45 ms. Cache key currently includes userId, timestamp and the full query string.

GET /v1/suggest?q=iph&limit=5&lang=en&userId=42&_=1731150000123
Cache-Control: no-store
questions.promptHtml: How do you cut cost without hurting latency or quality?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add more servers or a bigger CDN plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How personalised are results really? Is staleness of a few minutes OK?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop the timestamp param and no-store; set Cache-Control: public, max-age=300 for the shared part.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cache key fragmentation (userId, timestamp); wrong cache headers; short prefixes not cached at the edge.
  4. How I'd verify each: CDN logs by key, hit ratio per prefix length.
  5. Root cause: Cache key includes values that make every request unique.
  6. Fix: Cache key = (prefix, lang, limit). Personalisation applied by re-ranking the top 20 from the shared index down to 5 at the edge or the client. Short prefixes (1 to 3 chars) have a few thousand keys serving most traffic, so hit rates of 90%+ are achievable. Client prefix cache and debounce/cancel.
  7. Prevention: Dashboard of hit ratio per layer; a test that asserts cache-key shape.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not personalise at the origin per request; that kills caching. Staleness up to 5 minutes is acceptable here.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Trending spike needs freshness? -> Short TTL for the overlay, or purge hot prefixes.
  • Privacy of personalised results? -> Keep them out of shared caches.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cache-buster parameter left in the client reduced CDN hit rate to 20% and doubled server cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more servers.
  • Hire: fixes cache key and headers.
  • Strong hire: personalisation via re-rank, per-layer metrics.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants "trending now" suggestions within 2 minutes of a spike (election night, a celebrity event). Current design rebuilds hourly. Engineering is split: (A) move the whole pipeline to streaming and rebuild every 2 minutes; (B) keep hourly snapshots and add a real-time overlay. Budget is limited; the index is 12 GB.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks A because "real-time is better".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What fraction of queries are trending? How strict is "2 minutes"? What is the cost of a bad trending suggestion?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Spikes affect a tiny part of the keyspace; the long tail is stable.
  4. How I'd verify each: Analyse a month of logs: share of top-K changes per hour; compute cost of 12 GB rebuilds every 2 minutes (720 builds/day and swaps).
  5. Root cause: N/A.
  6. Fix: B: keep immutable hourly snapshots; add a streaming job (Flink) with a Count-Min sketch plus a heap of spiking queries (spike ratio vs baseline), merged into the top-K at request time. The overlay is tiny (thousands of entries).
  7. Prevention: Safety filters apply to overlay too; limit overlay entries; A/B test by click-through.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: B is a two-way door; it can be disabled. A is costly and makes rollback of a bad build harder. I would not skip filtering for trending items, which are the riskiest.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Sketch memory? -> Small, fixed; tens of MB.
  • Overlay false positives (spam bursts)? -> Minimum unique-user thresholds.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A breaking-news term appeared in suggestions before moderation because trending bypassed the denylist.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: full streaming without reasons.
  • Hire: overlay with snapshots.
  • Strong hire: data-driven choice, reversibility and filtering of trends.

questions.contextHtml: The product expands from English to 30 languages. Index grows from 12 GB to 400 GB. Peak is 400k req/s globally, distributed over regions. One engineer proposes sharding by first character; another proposes sharding by language and region. Latency target stays p99 under 50 ms at the server.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Shards by first letter and merges results across shards.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Traffic per language? Do users mix languages? Where are the users?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: First-letter sharding creates hot shards ("s", "a" busy, "x" idle) and forces scatter-gather for ambiguous cases; language is a natural partition.
  4. How I'd verify each: Query distribution per language and per first letter from logs.
  5. Root cause: N/A.
  6. Fix: Partition by language/region; each partition is replicated (fits in memory, for example 13 GB average). Big languages get more replicas, small ones fewer. Within one huge language, if needed, prefix-range partitioning on a balanced split point (not by letter). Geo-routing sends users to nearby regions; unicode normalisation and per-language tokenisation in the build.
  7. Prevention: Per-partition QPS dashboards; automatic replica scaling.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not scatter-gather every keystroke across shards: latency is the maximum of all legs. Mixed-language queries need a router that picks 1 to 2 partitions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User types in two languages? -> Router consults the user's language set and merges two lists.
  • Cross-region replication cost? -> Snapshots are distributed through object storage, not live replication.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Sharding by first letter put 20% of traffic on the shard for "s" and the shard became the outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: first-letter sharding.
  • Hire: language/region partitions with replicas.
  • Strong hire: balanced prefix ranges, router for mixed queries, geo and replica planning.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident: a ranking change (recency boost x3) shipped with the 14:00 snapshot. Click-through on suggestions fell from 31% to 22% over 3 hours, and searches per session dropped 6%. It took 3 hours for anyone to notice; rollback took 20 minutes because snapshots were pruned to the last one only.

suggestion_ctr: 31% -> 22% (14:00 -> 17:00)
index_version: 2026-11-09-14 (prev snapshot deleted at 14:10)
alert: none configured on CTR

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Be more careful with ranking changes."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the change tested offline? Was there a canary? Who owns metrics?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back to the previous snapshot (rebuild from the old formula if needed).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Over-weighting recency promoted low-quality trending items; no gating or canary.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare top-K lists before and after for the top 1,000 prefixes; slice CTR by prefix length.
  5. Root cause: Ranking change went to 100% without an experiment, with no guard metric and no rollback artefact.
  6. Fix: Keep the last 3 snapshots; staged rollout (1% canary, A/B on CTR and searches per session); automatic rollback if CTR drops by more than X%; offline evaluation with replayed logs.
  7. Prevention: CTR alert, change review for ranking formulas, version labels on responses for debugging.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not tie rollback to rebuilds; storing three snapshots is cheap (about 36 GB). I would not rely on humans noticing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• CTR can fall for external reasons? -> A/B control group isolates the cause.
  • Personalisation experiments? -> Segment by user cohort with privacy review.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A recency boost promoted clickbait queries, and the lost 3 hours of CTR were the cheapest part of the cost; trust in suggestions fell for days.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: vague "be careful".
  • Hire: canary, rollback artefacts, alert.
  • Strong hire: A/B guardrails, offline evaluation, auto-rollback and snapshot retention reasoning.
